Q: Store Tesseract Output in PDF using R A:

I created a new Rcpp binding for tesseract. The code is available here with the installaction code : https://github.com/ManuHamel/rtesseract. You can use this code to convert a scanned pdf to a searchable PDF or an image to a searchable PDF :

library(rtesseract)
library(pdftools)

eng <- tess_open(
  language = "eng",
  datapath = "C:/rtools45/ucrt64/share/tessdata/"
)

tess_searchable_pdf_from_images(
  eng,
  image_paths = c("lnCHO.png"),
  output_pdf = "output1.pdf",
  dpi = 300
)

tess_searchable_pdf_from_scanned_pdf(
  eng,
  input_pdf = "D:\\scan.pdf",
  output_pdf = "D:\\scan_ocr.pdf",
  dpi = 300
)

pdf_text("D:\\scan_ocr.pdf")
[1] "Some text in an image for\nuse in testing tesseract\nand OCR.\n"

Q: Which programming tool can best help beginners learn? A:

i would recommend something like sublime text if you are just starting. it is super easy to understand and to use, it is the only non ide code editor i use frequently. just remember to get a compiler for your programming language and read up on how to use it :)

as for learning coding itself, (in the future) if you are more into hands on coding, i would recommend either:

CS50 - it is a bit challenging, consisting of 10 weeks of material (youtube lectures, 10 problem sets with small logic challenges that will actually make you feel the dopamine when you finish one) and it gives you a certificate at the end, and actually teaches you fundamentals very very well. you can continue learning your own field which you will (hopefully!) pick by then (such as backend, frontend, devops, all that)

FreeCodeCamp - also gives you a certificate at the end, i am not fully aware of the details so you will have to go look it up.

or if you like youtube vids:

Bro Code - very nice youtuber, likes pizza, has long 12 hour tutorials on python. he makes concepts i never understood before easy to understand, and also does many languages such as c, c++, c#, html, css, javascript and python (including numpy).

but pretty much any tutorial of your choice will do

have fun and good luck :)

Q: How can I remove/delete a large file from the commit history in the Git repository? A:

100 times faster than git filter-branch and easier to use

There are very good answers in this thread, but meanwhile many of them are outdated. Using git-filter-branch is no longer recommended, because it is difficult to use and awfully slow on big repositories with many commits.

git-filter-repo is much faster and easier to use.

git-filter-repo is a Python script, available at github: https://github.com/newren/git-filter-repo . When installed it looks like a regular git command and can be called by git filter-repo.

You need only one file: the Python3 script git-filter-repo. Copy it to a path that is included in the PATH variable. On Windows you may have to change the first line of the script (refer INSTALL.md). You need Python3 installed installed on your system, but this is not a big deal.

First you can run:

git filter-repo --analyze

This will generate some statistics files in .git/filter-repo/analysis/ that lists the git files by size. This helps you to determine what to do next.

You can delete your DVD-rip file or any other file like this:

git filter-repo --invert-paths --path DVD-rip

Filter-repo is really fast. A task that took around 9 hours on my computer by filter-branch, was completed in 4 minutes by filter-repo. You can do many more nice things with filter-repo. Refer to the documentation for that.

WARNING: Do this on a copy of your repository. Many actions of filter-repo cannot be undone. filter-repo will change the commit hashes of all modified commits (of course) and all their descendants down to the last commits!

Q: Node in Jenkins is offline although agent is connected in server A:

The Send Unexport right after a successful connection is the key clue here. It means the controller is accepting the TCP/SSL handshake but immediately tearing down the remoting channel. I've seen this exact pattern before — almost always comes down to a stale agent.jar.

Since your infra team was poking around the server (even if they say they didn't touch Jenkins), it's very likely that something changed on the controller side — a service restart, a Java update, a plugin auto-update — that bumped the expected remoting version. Your agents are still running the old agent.jar, so the controller connects, realizes there's a mismatch, and sends Unexport to kill the channel.

First thing to try: Re-download agent.jar on every agent machine directly from your controller:


curl -o agent.jar <your_jenkins_url>/jnlpJars/agent.jar

Then relaunch. This fixes it ~90% of the time when all nodes go offline simultaneously.

If that doesn't fix it, check these:

  1. Java version mismatch — Run java -version on the agent machines. If infra updated Java on the server or the agents, you might have a compatibility issue. Recent Jenkins versions require Java 11+.

  2. Agent port / firewall changes — JNLP4 needs the agent port (the one showing in your "Agent discovery successful" output) to be open bidirectionally. Infra "fixing slowness" sometimes means tightening firewall rules.

  3. Corrupted work directory — You mentioned heavy parallel Chrome automation. Try clearing out the agent work directories and relaunching fresh.

You can also relaunch with -agentLog agent-debug.log to get a more detailed log on the agent side showing the exact rejection reason.

The fact that all nodes died at once pretty much rules out individual node issues — it's something global on the controller side. The Chrome parallel load is probably a red herring for the offline issue itself, but it might be what triggered the infra team to make changes that broke things.

Q: How to handle LONGBLOB-type fields in gbase database? A:

Yes, you can extract the spatial value directly via SQL using MySQL's built-in JSON functions. Since your column is LONGBLOB, you need to convert it to text first before applying JSON path extraction.

Solution:

SELECT 
  JSON_UNQUOTE(
    JSON_EXTRACT(
      CONVERT(properties USING utf8mb4),
      '$.value.spatial'
    )
  ) AS spatial_value
FROM your_table;

Or using the shorter ->> operator (MySQL 5.7.13+):

SELECT 
  CONVERT(properties USING utf8mb4) ->> '$.value.spatial' AS spatial_value
FROM your_table;

Key points:

  • CONVERT(properties USING utf8mb4) is needed because JSON_EXTRACT expects text/JSON input, not raw LONGBLOB bytes.
  • $.value.spatial is the JSON path — $ is root, .value navigates into the nested object, .spatial targets the field.
  • JSON_UNQUOTE() (or the ->> shorthand) strips the surrounding double quotes from the result, giving you the plain string POINT(109.04604121405723 31.305242240075117) instead of "POINT(...)".
  • Requires MySQL 5.7+ for JSON functions.

Tip: If you query this column frequently, consider changing the type from LONGBLOB to JSON — you'll get native validation, skip the CONVERT step, and can even create virtual generated columns with indexes for faster lookups.
